threat: A provider-supplied endpoint or a stored connection causes a server-side request to a private/internal destination (SSRF).
strengths: There is a real, centralized, defense-in-depth SSRF design rather than a single check. The URL guard (Kernel/API/src/core/url.ts) enforces HTTPS for every remote provider URL and allows cleartext http: only to loopback hostnames; it rejects userinfo, blocks private IP text at save time and again on every request via isPrivateHostname() (a broad list: 0/8, 10/8, 127/8, 172.16-31, 192.168, 192.0.0/24 incl. the 192.0.0.192 metadata host, 169.254/16, 100.64/10 CGNAT, 198.18-19, 224/4+, plus .local/.internal, IPv6 fc/fd/fe80-fe bf, ::1 and ::), and handles the non-obvious bypasses: a trailing DNS dot, decimal/hex IP spellings normalized by the WHATWG URL parser, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (https://[::ffff:169.254.169.254] normalizes to [::ffff:a9fe:a9fe] and is unwrapped to 169.254.169.254 and refused). resolveProviderUrl() guards base-path escape and forbids scheme-relative/backslash paths; sanitizeProviderHeaders() blocks credential, CRLF and transport (Host, Content-Length, etc.) headers, and the transport uses redirect:'error' so an open-redirect cannot be used to pivot. Crucially, the gateway adds a request-time DNS check: FetchHttpTransport.request() and .stream() both call assertSafeProviderRequestUrl() and then await checkDestination via assertPublicDestination (Kernel/API/src/core/destination-check.ts), which resolves the host (bounded 2.5s system lookup, deduplicated in-flight, 60s verdict cache), judges every returned address, refuses on any private answer, and refuses names that do not resolve. That check is wired into both transports the gateway builds (the static registry in core/config.ts and the on-demand/generic resolver transport in core/service.ts), so a stored custom endpoint - including the synthesized OpenAICompatibleAdapter built for an unregistered provider in core/provider-resolver.ts - goes through it, and the SDK OpenAI-compatible adapter performs model discovery (/models) through the injected transport too (Kernel/SDK/openai/lib/openai-compatible.ts), not a raw fetch. Stored connections are re-validated on load and backup restore (normalizeInput -> assertSafeProviderRequestUrl), and at request time regardless. All other server-side fetches in routes go to fixed first-party URLs (DuckDuckGo search, GitHub releases, ChatGPT first-party origin guard in chatgptFirstParty.ts, OpenCode Console, ZCode OAuth), and message image_url values are only text-checked and forwarded to the provider, not downloaded locally. Tests are strong and measured against real listeners: private-destinations.test.js pins the full range list and the IPv4-mapped metadata case, destination-check.test.js runs a local stub DNS to prove nip.io->loopback is refused, a public answer allowed, a non-resolving name refused, cache on/off behavior, and that the user-facing error names the private-address cause; transport.test.js-style assertions cover the guard, and SECURITY.md / docs/SPEC-SDK.md document the boundary explicitly.
weaknesses: The central residual is the one the code itself documents and does not fix: check/connect are two separate DNS resolutions. assertPublicDestination() validates one lookup, then global fetch resolves the host again on connect; an authoritative DNS for a provider-supplied endpoint that answers public to the check and private to the connection wins the race, so a stored https://attacker-controlled.example endpoint can be rebound to loopback/an internal address (the 60s verdict cache widens the window). Closing it needs a connect-time/pinned-IP policy that Node's global fetch does not expose; SECURITY.md:153-156 records this as an accepted limitation and docs/SPEC-SDK.md:93 still describes the older text-only state. Related to this, resolveForDestinationCheck()'s public-rescue discards a private system answer whenever the system set is all-private (systemIsAllPrivate ? published : [...]), contradicting its own 'refuse on any private answer' rule: a hostname remapped to a private IP locally (/etc/hosts or local DNS) but public on 8.8.8.8 is judged public and allowed, while the actual fetch still uses the local resolver and connects to the private IP. The cleartext exemption is broad by design: isLoopbackHostname() accepts all of 127.0.0.0/8 and ::1, and a stored connection may point http:// at any loopback port (Ollama is the intended case), so the gateway will perform server-side requests to arbitrary loopback services. The private-literal check is text/prefix based and misses IPv6 transition prefixes that embed IPv4 (6to4 2002::/16, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, Teredo), and only .local/.internal are suffix-blocked rather than a fuller internal-name list; in practice the request-time DNS check catches most of these once resolved, but it does not catch loopback (exempt) or a successful rebind. checkDestination is optional on the SDK FetchHttpTransport and defaults to absent, so any embedder that constructs its own transport (or an SDK adapter built with no transport) sends requests with no DNS check - the gateway always supplies one, but the safety is not enforced by the type. Finally, parseImageUrl() (routes/inference.ts) is text-only with no DNS resolution; I found no local download of image URLs (they are forwarded to the provider), so this is not a live gateway SSRF, but it is a weaker check than the transport's and a future adapter that downloads images would inherit that gap. Net: strong against literal private endpoints, DNS names that currently resolve private, redirects, header injection and path escape; not a guarantee against an attacker-controlled DNS name or loopback, which is exactly the 'provider-supplied endpoint' case in the threat.
